lead: This unit moves from flat plates to stiffened panels, crippling and composite laminates, then to vibration and aeroelasticity. After it you can find plate bending moments, critical buckling loads, effective sheet width, crippling and torsional buckling strength, laminate A, B, D stiffness, natural frequency and shear-plus-compression buckling limits.
about: The unit starts with 6.1, pure bending of thin plates, and fixes the moment–curvature relation for a Kirchhoff plate. 6.2 adds transverse pressure and in-plane loads. 6.3 turns in-plane compression into an eigenvalue buckling problem, and 6.4 uses that result for stiffened panels and effective sheet width. 6.5 covers local buckling and crippling by Needham and Gerard methods. 6.6 treats flexural–torsional buckling of open thin-walled columns. 6.7 introduces orthotropic FRP plies, and 6.8 builds the laminate A, B, D stiffness matrix and composite beam EI. 6.9 gives vibration and aeroelasticity basics. 6.10 closes with shear and combined-load plate buckling.

chapters.idea: A thin plate resists bending through curvature, and its moment–curvature relation is set by the plate stiffness D.
chapters.depth: Kirchhoff assumptions, small deflection w(x,y), curvatures κx=−∂²w/∂x², κy=−∂²w/∂y², twisting curvature κxy=−2∂²w/∂x∂y, moment–curvature relations, D=Et³/[12(1−ν²)] with E, t and ν, anticlastic and synclastic surfaces, cylindrical bending. Only a few universities teach the full derivation; others give the results.

figure.title: Thin plate bending
figure.caption: Curvature of the mid-surface creates bending and twisting moments; D sets their size.
figure.aria: Block diagram from deflection to curvatures to moments, using plate stiffness D.

chapters.example: A 3 mm aluminium plate has E=70 GPa and ν=0.30. It is bent cylindrically with κx=0.05 m⁻¹ and κy=−νκx. Find D, Mx, My and the maximum bending stress. Answer: D=173.1 N·m, Mx=7.88 N·m/m, My=0, σmax=5.25 MPa.
chapters.trap: Using EI instead of D and dropping the factor (1−ν²); also mixing the sign convention for anticlastic curvature.
chapters.prereq: Unit 4 bending of thin-walled beams; basic strength of materials.
chapters.leave: Large-deflection plate theory and finite-element plate elements.

chapters.idea: Transverse pressure and in-plane forces both enter the plate equation, so bending and membrane action combine.
chapters.depth: Governing biharmonic equation ∇⁴w=q/D; Navier and Levy solutions for rectangular plates; simply supported and clamped edges; combined bending and in-plane loading; membrane stress resultants Nx, Ny and Nxy. Some syllabi call this plates under bending, twisting and transverse loads.

figure.title: Combined plate loading
figure.caption: Lateral pressure drives bending; in-plane forces add a membrane term that can stiffen or soften the plate.
figure.aria: Block diagram showing lateral load and in-plane load entering the plate equation to give deflection and stress.

chapters.example: A square simply supported plate is 800 mm × 800 mm × 4 mm, with E=70 GPa, ν=0.30 and q=1 kPa. Find D and the maximum deflection. Answer: D=410.3 N·m; wmax=0.00406 q a⁴/D=4.05 mm. If Nx=10 kN/m compression acts, the uniaxial buckling load from 6.3 is Ncr=25.3 kN/m, so Nx/Ncr=0.395.
chapters.trap: Forgetting that D contains (1−ν²), and treating an in-plane compressive load as a harmless addition rather than a buckling precursor.
chapters.leave: The buckling eigenvalue itself to 6.3; shear buckling to 6.10.

chapters.idea: A thin plate becomes unstable when in-plane compressive membrane forces do work against a small bending mode.
chapters.depth: Derive D∇⁴w+Nx w,xx+2Nxy w,xy+Ny w,yy=0; simply supported edges; buckling coefficient k; Ncr=kπ²D/b²; mode shapes with m half-waves; aspect ratio effect; structural instability. Some syllabi call this the governing equation for plate buckling.

figure.caption: Lowest branch gives the critical buckling coefficient k for a simply supported plate in uniaxial compression.
figure.aria: Plot of plate buckling coefficient k against aspect ratio a/b for three half-wave numbers.

chapters.example: A simply supported plate has a=1.2 m, b=0.6 m, t=3 mm, E=70 GPa and ν=0.30. It is compressed along x. Find k and the critical load per unit width. Answer: D=173.1 N·m; a/b=2, so m=2 gives k=4; Ncr=4π²D/b²=18.98 kN/m; σcr=Ncr/t=6.33 MPa.
chapters.trap: Using Euler's column formula; plate buckling depends on b, edge restraint and mode number, not only on length.
chapters.prereq: 6.2; Unit 3 Euler columns for the instability idea.
chapters.leave: Post-buckling strength and stiffened panel effective width to 6.4; shear and combined loading to 6.10.

chapters.idea: After the skin buckles between stringers, only a limited effective width of sheet still acts with each stiffener.
chapters.depth: Compression panels; skin buckling between stringers; effective sheet width b_eff=C t√(E/σ); shear lag; boom-panel idealisation; effective area per stiffener A_eff=A_st+2b_eff t. Some syllabi call this sheet effective width or effective width concept.

figure.title: Effective sheet width
figure.caption: The buckled skin is replaced by an effective width of sheet working with each stringer.
figure.aria: Block diagram from compressed skin to stringer support, local skin buckling and effective width.

chapters.example: A stiffened panel has stringer area 200 mm², skin thickness 1.5 mm and E=70 GPa. At skin stress 100 MPa the effective-width constant is 1.9. Find b_eff on each side and effective area per stringer. Answer: b_eff=1.9×0.0015×√(70×10⁹/100×10⁶)=75.4 mm; A_eff=200+2×75.4×1.5=426.2 mm².
chapters.trap: Using the full sheet width after buckling; the effective width is a reduced width, not the stiffener pitch.
chapters.prereq: 6.3; Unit 5 shear flow, booms and panels.
chapters.leave: Crippling of the stiffener itself to 6.5; shear lag in closed boxes to Unit 5.

chapters.idea: Thin compression elements buckle locally and fail by crippling at a stress below yield; Needham and Gerard estimate that stress.
chapters.depth: Local buckling of flange and web elements; crippling stress; Needham empirical curves; Gerard semi-empirical method; inter-rivet buckling and sheet wrinkling; cut-off at compressive yield σcy. Use the chart or coefficients supplied in the question; do not assume one universal formula.

figure.caption: Crippling charts give a stress ratio below yield; the marked point is b/t=15 with ratio 0.60.
figure.aria: Plot of crippling stress ratio against b/t with one example point and a yield cut-off line.

chapters.example: A 2024-T3 angle has σcy=320 MPa, b/t=15 and area A=180 mm². The Gerard chart gives σcrip/σcy=0.60. Find the crippling load. Answer: σcrip=0.60×320=192 MPa; Pcrip=192×10⁶×180×10⁻⁶=34.6 kN.
chapters.trap: Using the elastic local buckling stress as the crippling stress; crippling includes post-local-buckling and yielding effects.
chapters.leave: Flexural–torsional column buckling to 6.6; full post-buckling analysis.

chapters.idea: An open thin-walled column can buckle by bending and twisting together because the load line and shear centre do not coincide.
chapters.depth: Open thin-walled columns; shear centre offset; torsion constant J; warping constant Cw; polar radius r0²=(Ix+Iy)/A+x0²+y0²; torsional buckling load Pt=(GJ+π²ECw/L²)/r0²; coupled flexural–torsional equation. Only a few universities teach this at derivation level. Some syllabi call this torsional instability of thin-walled columns.

figure.title: Flexural–torsional buckling
figure.caption: When the load acts away from the shear centre, bending and twist couple and lower the buckling load.
figure.aria: Block diagram from centroid and shear centre offset to coupled bending and twisting buckling.

chapters.example: A channel column has A=400 mm², Ix+Iy=640000 mm⁴, y0=20 mm, G=27 GPa, J=200 mm⁴, E=70 GPa, Cw=1.2×10⁸ mm⁶ and L=800 mm. Find the torsional buckling load. Answer: r0²=640000/400+20²=2000 mm²; GJ=5.4×10⁶ N·mm²; π²ECw/L²=129.5×10⁶ N·mm²; Pt=(134.9×10⁶)/2000=67.5 kN.
chapters.trap: Taking moments about the centroid instead of the shear centre; ignoring warping stiffness Cw for open sections.
chapters.prereq: Unit 5 torsion of thin-walled open sections; 6.3.
chapters.leave: Vibration and flutter to 6.9; detailed finite-element buckling.

chapters.idea: A fibre-reinforced ply is orthotropic: its stiffness along the fibres differs from that across the fibres.
chapters.depth: FRP fibre and matrix; orthotropic lamina; principal axes 1,2; E1, E2, ν12, G12; reduced stiffness Q11=E1/(1−ν12ν21), Q22=E2/(1−ν12ν21), Q12=ν12E2/(1−ν12ν21), Q66=G12; transformation Qbar(θ). Only a few universities teach this.

figure.title: Orthotropic ply
figure.caption: An orthotropic ply has different stiffness along and across the fibres; rotation gives Qbar for laminate axes.
figure.aria: Block diagram from fibre and matrix directions to ply constants, Q matrix and rotated Qbar.

chapters.example: A carbon/epoxy ply has E1=140 GPa, E2=10 GPa, ν12=0.30 and G12=5 GPa. Find Q11, Q22, Q12 and Q66. Answer: ν21=ν12E2/E1=0.02143; denominator=1−ν12ν21=0.99357; Q11=140.9 GPa; Q22=10.07 GPa; Q12=3.02 GPa; Q66=5 GPa.
chapters.trap: Using E1 directly without the (1−ν12ν21) factor; mixing ν12 and ν21; using degrees where the transformation needs radians.
chapters.prereq: Unit 1 aerospace materials and their behaviour.
chapters.leave: Stacking plies into a laminate to 6.8; failure criteria to later study.

chapters.idea: A laminate is built by summing each rotated ply through the thickness to give extensional, coupling and bending stiffness matrices.
chapters.depth: Classical laminate theory; A, B, D matrices; Aij=ΣQbar(zk−zk−1), Bij=½ΣQbar(zk²−zk−1²), Dij=⅓ΣQbar(zk³−zk−1³); symmetric laminate B=0; composite beam EI=bD11; stacking sequence and mid-plane reference.

figure.caption: A symmetric cross-ply laminate; the mid-plane is the reference z=0.
figure.aria: Stack of four plies in a symmetric 0/90/90/0 laminate with thickness coordinates.

chapters.example: A [0/90]s laminate has four plies, each 0.125 mm thick. Q11=140.9 GPa and Q22=10.1 GPa. Find A11, D11 per unit width and EI for a 100 mm wide beam. Answer: A11=2(140.9)(0.125)+2(10.1)(0.125)=37.75 GPa·mm=37750 N/mm; D11=1297 N·mm; EI=bD11=100×1297=1.30×10⁵ N·mm². B11=0 because the laminate is symmetric.
chapters.trap: Using Q instead of Qbar for the 90° plies; forgetting that z is measured from the mid-plane; expecting B=0 for an unsymmetric laminate.
chapters.leave: Aeroelastic tailoring and detailed failure analysis to 6.9 and later study.

chapters.idea: Every structure has natural frequencies and damping, and aeroelastic coupling can cause divergence or flutter.
chapters.depth: SDOF vibration; ωn=√(k/m); damping ratio ζ=c/(2√(km)); modes; lumped models for continuous systems; static divergence and dynamic flutter; reduced frequency.

figure.caption: Resonance peak at r=1; damping limits the amplitude.
figure.aria: Plot of vibration amplitude against frequency ratio for damping ratio 0.2.

chapters.example: A wing model has mass m=500 kg and stiffness k=200 kN/m. Find the natural frequency. With damping c=4000 N·s/m, find ζ. Answer: ωn=√(200000/500)=20 rad/s; fn=20/(2π)=3.18 Hz; ζ=4000/(2√(200000×500))=0.20.
chapters.trap: Reporting rad/s as Hz; forgetting the 2π; confusing divergence (static) with flutter (dynamic).
chapters.prereq: Unit 2 energy methods; 6.8 for composite stiffness.
chapters.leave: Unsteady aerodynamics and detailed flutter solution.

chapters.idea: Shear and combined compression–shear loading buckle a plate at lower loads, and their interaction follows a curve rather than a simple sum.
chapters.depth: Shear buckling coefficient ks; Nxy,cr=ksπ²D/b²; interaction with compression; combined loading curves; post-buckling diagonal tension mentioned. Some syllabi call this buckling due to shear and combined loading.

figure.caption: Interaction curve for compression plus shear; the marked point is the worked example.
figure.aria: Plot of shear load ratio against compression load ratio with a quadratic interaction curve and one example point.

chapters.example: A simply supported square plate is 800 mm × 800 mm × 4 mm, with E=70 GPa and ν=0.30. Find the shear buckling load. If Nx=10 kN/m compression also acts, find the allowable shear. Answer: D=410.3 N·m; ks=9.34; Nxy,cr=9.34π²D/b²=59.1 kN/m; Nx,cr=25.3 kN/m; interaction (10/25.3)²+(Nxy/59.1)²=1 gives Nxy=54.3 kN/m.
chapters.trap: Adding compression and shear directly; using the wrong ks for edge restraint; ignoring post-buckling diagonal tension.
chapters.leave: Tension-field web beams and Wagner theory to Unit 5.
